title: Gap in $r$-dependence of sign-pattern bound
statement_text: For tuples of $m$ functions on $\mathbb{R}^N$, each a linear combination of at most $r$ terms $g^{1/s}$ with $g$ a polynomial of degree at most $\Delta$ that is nonnegative on $\mathbb{R}^N$, the number of distinct proper sign patterns is at most $2(2s^{r-2}\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N 2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$, which is exponential in $r$. Any such bound must have at least a linear dependence on $r$ if it is to depend polynomially on $m$. It would be interesting to close this gap.
context_text: For a tuple $\mathcal{F}=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of real functions on $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$, the sign pattern of $x$ is $(\mathrm{sgn} f_1(x),\dots,\mathrm{sgn} f_m(x))\in\{0,1,-1\}^m$, and it is proper if no entry is $0$. Warren's theorem bounds the number of proper sign patterns of $m$ polynomials of degree at most $\Delta$ in $N$ variables by $2(2\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$. As an analogue, the authors prove that if each $f_i$ is of the form $\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}a_{i,j}g_{i,j}^{1/s}$ with $r_i\le r$ ($r\ge2$), real coefficients $a_{i,j}$ and polynomials $g_{i,j}$ of degree at most $\Delta$ that are nonnegative on $\mathbb{R}^N$, then the number of proper sign patterns is at most $2(2s^{r-2}\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$, a bound exponential in $r$. They use it to count the orderings of a set of candidate points by the sum of Euclidean distances to $k$ vantage points. The authors show that the dependence on $r$ cannot be removed: with $N=1$ and $\Delta=s=2$ fixed, the functions $f_{\vec a}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_i\big(\sqrt{(x-i)^2+\delta^2}-\sqrt{(x-i)^2}\big)$ with $\vec a\in\{-1,1\}^\ell$ and small $\delta>0$ satisfy $\mathrm{sgn} f_{\vec a}(j)=a_j$ for $j\in[\ell]$, so with $\ell=2^m$ one obtains $m$ such functions with $r=2^{m+1}$ realizing all $2^m$ proper sign patterns. Informally, this forces at least a linear dependence on $r$ for a bound polynomial in $m$, far below the exponential dependence of their bound. This is real algebraic geometry rather than graph theory.
notes: Stated informally in prose; no labelled environment.

title: Gap in connected-component count for sums of square roots
statement_text: For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ a linear combination of $r$ square roots of everywhere-positive quadratic polynomials, the number of connected components of $\mathbb{R} \setminus V(f)$ is at most $2^{r-1}+1$, while at least $2r-1$ components are achievable. It would be interesting to narrow the gap between this linear lower bound and the exponential upper bound.
context_text: For a tuple $\mathcal{F}=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of real functions on $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$, the sign pattern of $x$ is $(\mathrm{sgn} f_1(x),\dots,\mathrm{sgn} f_m(x))\in\{0,1,-1\}^m$, and it is proper if no entry is $0$. Warren's theorem bounds the number of proper sign patterns of $m$ polynomials of degree at most $\Delta$ in $N$ variables by $2(2\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$. As an analogue, the authors prove that if each $f_i$ is of the form $\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}a_{i,j}g_{i,j}^{1/s}$ with $r_i\le r$ ($r\ge2$), real coefficients $a_{i,j}$ and polynomials $g_{i,j}$ of degree at most $\Delta$ that are nonnegative on $\mathbb{R}^N$, then the number of proper sign patterns is at most $2(2s^{r-2}\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$, a bound exponential in $r$. They use it to count the orderings of a set of candidate points by the sum of Euclidean distances to $k$ vantage points. This is a simpler companion problem with $N=m=1$ and $\Delta=s=2$: for $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ a linear combination of $r$ square roots of everywhere-positive quadratic polynomials, the number of proper sign patterns is trivially at most $2$, so one counts instead the connected components of $\mathbb{R}\setminus V(f)$, where $V(f)=\{x: f(x)=0\}$ is the zero set. A multiplication-by-conjugates argument, as in the proof of their sign-pattern bound, gives at most $2^{r-1}+1$ components, while $f(x)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}(-1)^ia_i^{1/10}\big(\sqrt{x^2+a_i^2}-a_i\big)$ with $0<a_1<\dots<a_{r-1}$ growing extremely quickly has $2r-1$ components. This is real algebraic geometry rather than graph theory.

title: Five-point protrusive-but-not-witnessed construction
statement_text: Does there exist a set $C$ of $5$ points such that some protrusive ordering of $C$ is not in $\Psi(C)$?
context_text: For a set $C=\{c_1,\dots,c_n\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ of candidate points and a finite multiset $V=\{v_1,\dots,v_k\}$ of vantage points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $D_V(x)=\sum_{i}\|x-v_i\|$ (Euclidean distance). If the values $D_V(c_1),\dots,D_V(c_n)$ are distinct, $V$ witnesses the ordering of $C$ by increasing $D_V$. $\Psi(C)$ is the set of orderings of $C$ witnessed by some finite multiset $V$ (of any size). A tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is protrusive if for every $i<n$ the point $x_{i+1}$ is not in the convex hull of $x_1,\dots,x_i$. By the triangle inequality every ordering in $\Psi(C)$ is protrusive, and the authors prove that $\Psi(C)$ is exactly the set of protrusive orderings of $C$ when $d=1$, when $|C|\le4$, and when $C$ is the vertex set of a vertex-transitive polytope. In the other direction they construct a $6$-point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (the vertices of an equilateral triangle together with three points just outside the midpoints of its sides, in convex position) for which some protrusive ordering is not in $\Psi(C)$, and ask whether $5$ points suffice. The formal question does not fix the dimension; the $6$-point example is planar. This is combinatorial geometry rather than graph theory.
